                                            PROJECT NO. 58481

    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                              §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                           §
    STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                       §                    OF TEXAS

                                   COMMENTS OF
                    TRANSMISSION SERVICE PROVIDER COOPERATIVES

           Brazos Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Golden Spread Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Rayburn

Country Electric Cooperative, Inc.; and South Texas Electric Cooperative, Inc. (the “TSP

Cooperatives”) respectfully submit these comments in response to the proposal for publication

(“PFP”) regarding large load interconnection standards.1 The TSP Cooperatives provide

generation and/or transmission services to their members which are distribution cooperatives that

provide retail electric service to their end-use member-consumers. The PFP directed comments to

be filed by April 17; therefore, these comments are timely filed. The TSP Cooperatives generally

support comments of the Texas Electric Cooperatives (“TEC”) and also respond separately to

provide the perspective of electric cooperatives which provide transmission service.

                                                I.       Comments

           1. Applicability Clarification

           The TSP Cooperatives recommend that proposed subsection §25.194(b) be clarified.2 The

rule should provide clarity regarding which large loads currently under development will be

subject to the new requirements and the cutoff date for applicability. A number of factors could be

considered for applicability, including energization status, initiation of the study process,

completion of studies, etc. The TSP Cooperatives do not take a position as to the applicability

criteria and date, other than suggesting that these items should be established within the PFP, and


1
    Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC §25.194 (Mar. 12, 2026) (“PFP”).
2
    PFP at 7.


                                                                                                 1
 not an ERCOT process such as the process proposed by PGRR 145, and careful consideration

should be given to adopting retroactive requirements that could disrupt existing developing

projects that might not have achieved a specific milestone in the past. The PFP should also clarify

applicability in the event that a large load and a generation facility, which are not operating

together as a private use network, will share the same interconnection facilities but will have

separate metering and be separate transmission customers (i.e., the generator has no commercial

relationship with the load or with any other entity providing retail service to the load and the load

and generation would not be net-metered). With both independent transmission customers

interconnecting at the same facilities, how should the transmission costs be apportioned?

       The phrase “an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more” in

subsection (b)(3) could be interpreted to require that the expansion itself be at least 75 MW to

trigger §25.194, allowing existing large loads to expand repeatedly in increments below 75 MW

without meeting these requirements. Alternatively, it could be interpreted to require compliance

for any expansion once an interconnection exceeds 150 MW. In any event, it will create unintended

incentives for loads to piecemeal increases in demand so as to avoid the requirements, which would

have the unintended consequence of harming grid reliability as additional large load demand

increases below the threshold level. Loads may also seek separate interconnection for multiple

facilities on the same parcel with <75 MW demand, effectively avoiding the SB 6 requirements

altogether. Additionally, there is also no limitation on large loads that exceed their contracted peak

demand, or that utilize transmission capacity intended for other loads, and create congestion.

       On the other hand, under subsection (h)(1), if a large load is any de minimis amount below

its contracted peak demand six months after its required contract peak demand deadline or

milestone ramp deadline, the TSP or DSP is required to draw down on security. There is no option




                                                                                                    2
 for the large load to make a compensatory payment for other customers reflecting the slightly

reduced use of the system, even though the peak demand and ramp schedule cannot be precisely

defined.



       2. Multiple TSPs

       The TSP Cooperatives support TEC’s comments about the need for involvement of the

associated DSP in the interconnection process and agreements. Additionally, the TSP Cooperatives

recommend that the rule acknowledge that more than one TSP could be involved in the

interconnection with a large load. The TSP that has the line located nearest the proposed large load

may be different than the TSP that ultimately builds the facilities that directly interconnect with

the large load. This is a common scenario in areas where a TSP’s lines cross the service territory

of a distribution cooperative. In that situation, the TSP charged with the construction of the line

would likely be tasked with performing some studies, but the transmission cooperative responsible

for serving the distribution cooperative would ultimately provide the interconnection with the large

load, unless the large load connects at distribution voltage. Both TSPs would have costs associated

with interconnecting the large load. The rule needs to be clear which entities will perform which

studies or direct ERCOT to adopt procedures to identify those responsibilities. Absent an

agreement between TSPs, no TSP should be required to provide financial security or other

financial commitment to another TSP for the costs to interconnect a large load. Each TSP should

be required to interface directly with the large load customer, absent an agreement with the other

TSP, to collect financial security, contribution in aid of construction or other financial commitment

from the large load that is necessary to secure its expected costs. This is particularly important

since the studied improvements may change and the TSP with a change in estimated costs can




                                                                                                   3
 obtain more efficiently an increase in posted credit from the large load without having to have the

interconnecting TSP be the middleman acting as a collection agent for another TSP. It should be

at the option of the interconnecting TSP to determine whether it collects the security for other

TSPs or whether the large load must post directly with the other TSPs performing the upgrades. In

any event, a large load interconnection agreement should require that the large load would be in

default if it refuses to post credit required by the interconnecting TSP or another TSP that is

constructing improvements benefiting the large load.



       3. Non-refundable Funds Exceeding TSP Costs

       There are several situations in the current PFP that could result in a TSP collecting funds
in excess of the TSP’s costs:
           a. Non-refundable interconnection fee provided with execution of the
                interconnection agreement, 100% retained (subsection §25.194(f)(7))
           b. Withdrawal of all or a portion of peak demand, 80% of remaining funds retained
                (subsection §25.194(g)(4))
           c. Non-utilized capacity, 80% of remaining funds retained (subsection §25.194(h)(4))
           d. Withdrawal of all or a portion of peak demand, contribution in aid of construction
                (“CIAC”) is non-refundable (subsection §25.194(g)(5))
           e. Non-utilized capacity, CIAC is non-refundable (subsection §25.194(h)(5))



       For some of the instances identified above, the PFP instructs TSPs to use funds received

from the large load customer to offset their costs in rate base. For others, such as CIAC, however,

the accounting treatment is unclear. In either case, excess funds are problematic for the TSP

Cooperatives.

       The TSP Cooperatives are opposed to these provisions mandating rate base offsets, because

removing these costs entirely from rate base will prevent TSPs from earning a return on facilities



                                                                                                 4
 and equipment when the return of and on these facilities and equipment is statutorily authorized.

A TSP’s ability to earn a rate of return on its rate base is critical to its financial stability and its

ability to function as a TSP. These proposed large rate base offsets can significantly reduce the

overall rate base. In some cases where the rate base is smaller because the utility is smaller, a large

load that leaves the process and has its security credited to rate base may have the effect of

eliminating its rate base entirely, significantly weakening the utility’s financial standing and

contrary to statutory requirements that are designed to protect the financial health of these utilities.

A larger TSP may be similarly impacted by this requirement given the number of large loads which

have indicated interest in interconnection. For example, if a TSP signs interconnection agreements

for just ten large loads of 1,000 MW each, $500,000,000 in fees would be collected (10 X 1,000

MW X $50,000/MW). This could easily be more than some TDSPs’ rate bases.

       While the TSPs would still be collecting and keeping funds from the large load customers

pursuant to the PFP, use of these funds as proposed is far different from earning a rate of return on

rate base. A TSP would only be able to earn interest on the funds deposited, a percentage

significantly lower than the typical TSP rate of return. A TSP’s debt service requirements are based

upon expected rate recovery. A significant reduction in rate base may, therefore, lead to a violation

of a TSP’s loan covenants, putting its financing, and thus, its financial future, in jeopardy.

Additionally, the TSP would have insufficient funds to design, construct, maintain and operate its

system. The TSP would not have the ability to raise its rates to support its necessary activities

without a rate proceeding in front of the Commission that would seek funds from the very

customers the PUCT is seeking to protect. If a TSP must raise its rates to continue to operate, then

the benefit of any rate base offset would be defeated.




                                                                                                      5
            Recently, Commission Staff filed a memorandum in Project No. 59142 suggesting that

“The final draft of 16 TAC §25.194 should reflect that any withheld portion of financial

commitment should be applied to reducing a utility's annual revenue requirement rather than

reducing a utility's rate base.”3 Unfortunately, this suggestion does not solve all of the TSP

Cooperatives’ concerns. The administration of any sort of offset would be a significant additional

accounting burden for every TSP in the ERCOT region that received and has drawn down on the

security, or that received CIAC. The offset would require special accounting treatment and would

need to be recovered over the course of many years, given the potential magnitude. Even if the

amounts are applied against revenue requirements, accounting treatment questions remain: Will

these funds be treated as revenue? Will they be considered received from a nonmember, potentially

impacting a cooperative’s tax status? Will the reduction in normal TCOS revenues create potential

default scenarios with a TSP’s lender(s)? These impacts to the financial status of a cooperative

may impair the value and assumptions on which debt financing is based and ratings agencies rely.

           There is currently no accounting classification that allows for the treatment proposed by

Staff. Establishing a new ratemaking accounting classification and applying it to individual utilities

would require careful rulemaking, which cannot be done in time for the expected Batch Zero

process to commence. The consequences of getting this wrong could result in serious financial

issues for a TSP. The TSP Cooperatives, therefore, recommend that all funds in excess of a TSP’s

costs, whether related to security or CIAC, should be credited against the ERCOT Administrative

Fee. The ERCOT Administrative Fee has no “rate of return,” and it makes sense that ERCOT

collect the security and fees that will not be associated with TSP or DSP costs, and anything in

excess of ERCOT’s costs could be an ERCOT Administrative Fee credit, flowing ultimately to



3
    Staff Recommendations for Batch Zero at 3, Project No. 59142 (April 13, 2026)


                                                                                                    6
 each retail customer bill. The TSP Cooperatives understand Staff’s concern that a refundable

commitment will not ensure that a large load will energize. As discussed above, a non-refundable

commitment should not be applied to reduce rate base, but could be applied to the ERCOT

Administrative Fee and result in a credit to ERCOT loads. The Commission could initially have

these funds allocated through the ERCOT Administrative Fee but would have time to implement

a different allocation mechanism, via a rulemaking, for the revenues to be returned through

ERCOT to end-users other than through the ERCOT Administrative Fee.



        4. Contribution In Aid of Construction (CIAC) Provisions

        The TSP Cooperatives support TEC’s position regarding PURA §35.004 (c-2), which

specifically reinforces electric cooperatives’ and Municipally-Owned Utilities’ (MOUs) rights to

determine how they pass along large load interconnection costs.4 The TSP Cooperatives may opt

to charge CIAC as proposed in subsection §25.194(f)(9); however, they may prefer to hold

financial security until such time as costs have been incurred and then invoice the large load for

the actual costs incurred as CIAC. CIAC paid in advance of costs incurred, absent strong regulatory

provisions to the contrary, is likely to function much like a cash deposit in the event of a developer

bankruptcy. The rule should be clarified to allow optionality for electric cooperatives and MOUs

with respect to CIAC billings.

        The TSP Cooperatives also note that there is inconsistent treatment of CIAC in subsection

§25.194(f)(9)(C) as compared to subsections §25.194(g)(5) and (h)(5). If the CIAC is subject to




4
  PURA §35.004 (c-2) (“An electric cooperative or municipally owned utility that has not adopted customer choice
shall pass through to a large load customer who is subject to the standards adopted under Section 37.0561 the
reasonable costs to interconnect the large load in a manner determined by the electric cooperative or municipally
owned utility.” Emphasis Added).


                                                                                                               7
 true up, it looks more like a cash deposit. If the intention is that CIAC is nonrefundable, except in

the situation where facilities are completed and energized, that should be clearly stated.

       Finally, additional clarity is needed regarding the final treatment of the cost of significant

equipment or services as discussed in subsections §25.194(d)(l 1) and (f)(8) once facilities are

completed and energized. Presumably, the cost of the equipment should be assessed to the large

load customer (as with CIAC and in keeping with SB 6), but that is not clearly stated in the

proposed rule.



                                          II.      Conclusion

       The TSP Cooperatives appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed

rule and looks forward to working with the Commission and other stakeholders on this project.

Dated: April 17, 2026

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                                        OF TEXAS

                                 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The TSP Cooperatives strongly recommend the following:

   1) Proposed §25. 194(b) should clarify applicability, including which large loads currently
      under development will be subject to the new rules and on what date.
   2) The rule should allow a large load that does not materially miss its contracted peak demand
      or ramp schedule to pay an amount to make other customers whole rather than reallocating
      capacity when the large load has, in material part, met its commitment.
   3) Similarly, it should be clarified that increases or expansions of large loads should go
      through the process if the load is greater than 75 MW to avoid the unintended consequence
      of loads growing piecemeal, or dividing end-user sites into <75 MW parcels to avoid the
      niles.
   4) The rule should clarify responsibilities in interconnections with more than one TSP
      involved and prohibit one TSP from requiring security or financial commitment from
      another TSP for a large load interconnection.
   5) No forfeited security, fees, or CIAC in excess of the costs incurred by TSPs should be used
      as TSP rate base offsets. The proposed rule could instinct that these amounts are applied
      to the ERCOT Administrative Fee. Additional rulemaking activity could then be
      undertaken to establish a long-term approach to the handling of excess funds.
   6) Electric cooperatives’ use of CIAC should not be limited as proposed in the PFP, and CIAC
      treatment should be further clarified.

                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                     §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                 §                     OF TEXAS

                                 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The TSP Cooperatives strongly recommend the following:

   1) Proposed §25.194(b) should clarify applicability, including which large loads currently
      under development will be subject to the new rules and on what date.
   2) The rule should allow a large load that does not materially miss its contracted peak demand
      or ramp schedule to pay an amount to make other customers whole rather than reallocating
      capacity when the large load has, in material part, met its commitment.
   3) Similarly, it should be clarified that increases or expansions of large loads should go
      through the process if the load is greater than 75 MW to avoid the unintended consequence
      of loads growing piecemeal, or dividing end-user sites into <75 MW parcels to avoid the
      rules.
   4) The rule should clarify responsibilities in interconnections with more than one TSP
      involved and prohibit one TSP from requiring security or financial commitment from
      another TSP for a large load interconnection.
   5) No forfeited security, fees, or CIAC in excess ofthe costs incurred by TSPs should be used
      as TSP rate base offsets. The proposed rule could instruct that these amounts are applied
      to the ERCOT Administrative Fee. Additional rulemaking activity could then be
      undertaken to establish a long-term approach to the handling of excess funds.
   6) Electric cooperatives' use of CIAC should not be limited as proposed in the PFP, and CIAC
      treatment should be further clarified.
